symptom: food that sometimes felt stuck halfway down
hook: the gullet had twisted itself into a wine-bottle corkscrew
whatYouSee: The barium-filled oesophagus coils down the middle of the chest in tight repeating twists like a corkscrew.
whyItMatters: Diffuse oesophageal spasm causes chest pain that can mimic a heart attack and is relieved by GTN. A corkscrew oesophagus on barium swallow is highly suggestive of it.
treatment: Treatment targets the spasm once cardiac causes are excluded and may include smooth muscle relaxants such as nitrates or calcium channel blockers.
takeaway: Chest pain eased by GTN plus a corkscrew barium swallow points to the oesophagus and not the heart.

findings: Lateral projection fluoroscopic image of the chest and upper abdomen demonstrating a barium esophagram
The esophageal lumen is opacified with barium contrast throughout its entire visible length from the upper thoracic inlet to the gastroesophageal junction

The esophageal contour demonstrates a striking, regular, corrugated or corkscrew appearance with multiple simultaneous circular indentations producing a beaded or rosary-bead pattern along the entire length of the esophagus
The indentations are rhythmic, closely spaced, and symmetric, affecting the full circumference of the lumen
At the inferior extent, contrast pools into a globular collection consistent with the gastric fundus or cardia
The cervical esophagus at the top of the image appears relatively normal in caliber before the abnormal segmentation begins
No discrete fixed stricture, mass lesion, or mucosal destruction is identified
Thoracic spine is visible on the right with normal-appearing vertebral bodies; cardiac silhouette is partially visible on the left
No pneumomediastinum or extravasation of contrast is evident
differential: Diffuse esophageal spasm (DES): the classic corkscrew or rosary-bead appearance with multiple simultaneous non-peristaltic contractions is the hallmark finding and is the leading diagnosis

Nutcracker esophagus (now termed jackhammer esophagus / hypercontractile esophagus): can produce a similar corrugated appearance due to high-amplitude prolonged contractions, though typically fewer segments are involved

Presbyesophagus or tertiary contractions in the context of an esophageal motility disorder: diffuse non-propulsive tertiary contractions can produce a similar segmented appearance, particularly in older patients, and should be considered
anatomyConcerns: The corrugated pattern is physiologically implausible as a normal peristaltic wave; it represents simultaneous multi-segmental non-peristaltic contractions, which are pathological
The image appears to be a single static frame; a single frame cannot definitively distinguish simultaneous spasm from sequential tertiary waves without fluoroscopic real-time observation or manometry
No left-right anatomical marker is visible on the image, limiting definitive laterality confirmation

The globular pooling at the distal end could represent a prominent gastric fundus or could partly reflect a hiatal component; the gastroesophageal junction and diaphragmatic level are not clearly delineated

imageApproval.diagnosticReason: The classic corkscrew/rosary-bead pattern of multiple simultaneous deep alternating indentations along the entire thoracic oesophagus with smooth mucosa and no fixed stricture or mass is the hallmark fluoroscopic appearance of diffuse oesophageal spasm. The clinical vignette of intermittent dysphagia with food stuck halfway down is consistent. Nutcracker/jackhammer oesophagus could produce a similar appearance but typically involves fewer segments and higher amplitude; the diffuse, long-segment, tightly corrugated pattern here strongly favours DES over the alternatives. No laterality marker is present but this is an expected normal film feature. The distal pooling is consistent with contrast passing into the gastric fundus at the cardia.
